question: When the intended use of an AI system is listed in Annex III of the EU AI Act, the AI system is automatically high-risk, isn't it? If not, can you explain when that is not the case?

This exception does not apply where the system profiles natural persons. A system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk regardless of the four conditions. The provider must document this self-assessment before placing the system on the market. Even when the derogation applies, the provider must still register the system in the EU database for high-risk AI systems under Article 49(2) before placing it on the market or putting it into service.

pred_answer: Neither prohibited nor high-risk by virtue of the drone itself, an AI system does not acquire a risk tier from the aircraft that carries it; under Article 6 the tier turns on the AI's function and the product it forms part of, not on the fact that it flies. Using AI in a drone "to find who's around in town" changes that: identifying natural persons in a publicly accessible space is remote biometric identification, which falls within the biometrics use-case of Annex III and is therefore high-risk under Article 6(2); and in the narrower context of real-time remote biometric identification carried out by, or on behalf of, law enforcement authorities in publicly accessible spaces, the same operation crosses into a prohibited practice under Article 5 rather than being merely high-risk, the deciding facts being who operates it (law enforcement) and whether identification is in real time. Outside that law-enforcement scenario, the town-surveillance use remains high-risk on the Annex III biometrics route, and where the system interacts directly with the persons it processes it additionally attracts the Article 50 transparency duties. The toy character of the drone does not lower that classification: a biometric identification function is assessed on what it does under Annex III, so a toy drone that identifies people in a public space is high-risk (or, in the law-enforcement real-time case, prohibited under Article 5) on the same basis as any other platform. The toy status is relevant only on the separate Article 6(1) route, a toy is a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (the Toy Safety framework), so an AI system acting as a safety component of that product is high-risk only where the product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment; because the toy-safety regime generally permits internal control rather than third-party assessment, that route typically does not render the AI high-risk. Toy drones used for other applications follow the same deduction: where the on-board AI neither performs an Annex III use-case (such as biometrics) nor operates as a safety component of an Annex I product requiring third-party conformity assessment, it is not high-risk, and remains subject only to any applicable Article 50 transparency obligations and the general-purpose provisions that may attach to the underlying model.

question: Article 9 of the AI Act lists the five categories of harm that map to AI systems with: no risk, limited risk, high-risk, systemic risk, prohibited. What are the five categories and how do they map to the five risk levels?
pred_answer: The premise is inaccurate: Article 9 does not list five categories of harm, and the AI Act does not operate a single five-tier scale in which "systemic risk" sits alongside "no risk," "limited risk," "high-risk," and "prohibited." Article 9 (a cross-referenced provision here, not one of the operative classification articles) establishes the risk management system that a high-risk AI system must implement, document, and maintain throughout its lifecycle, it is an obligation that follows from classification, not the source of the classification taxonomy. Prohibited (unacceptable risk), governed by Article 5, which exhaustively bans eight categories of prohibited practice, including subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm and exploitation of vulnerabilities by age, disability or socio-economic situation. High-risk, governed by Article 6, on its two routes: a system is high-risk where it is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I, or where it falls within one of the Annex III use-case categories (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, and the others). High-risk status is what triggers the Chapter III obligations, including the Article 9 risk management system. Limited (transparency) risk, governed by Article 50, which imposes disclosure duties (informing natural persons they are interacting with an AI system; marking synthetic AI-generated content in a machine-readable, detectable format) without high-risk classification. So the correct mapping is a four-level risk pyramid for AI systems (prohibited → high-risk → limited/transparency → minimal), with systemic risk as a distinct fifth concept attaching to GPAI models rather than a tier of the AI-system pyramid, since it applies under Articles 51–55 to general-purpose AI models whose capabilities present systemic risk at Union level, regardless of how any downstream system built on them is classified.
